summary: The Hoysalas, hill chiefs of the Malnad in southern Karnataka, became a regional power when Vishnuvardhana drove the Cholas out of Gangavadi around 1116. Veera Ballala II threw off Chalukya overlordship around 1192, and his successors ruled the Kannada country and much of the Kaveri valley, with a second capital near Srirangam. Delhi armies sacked their capital Halebidu in 1311 and again around 1327; Veera Ballala III died fighting the Sultan of Madurai in 1343, and by 1346 the kingdom had passed to the new Vijayanagara state.
details: In the early 12th century the Hoysalas were a hill family of the Malnad region, nominally serving the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani. The Cholas held Gangavadi, the plateau around Talakad on the Kaveri, in what is now southern Karnataka. Vishnuvardhana, king from 1108, made its conquest his first great goal. His forces defeated the Chola general Adiyamma near Talakad, in 1116 according to the Hoysala Empire article, and Vishnuvardhana took the title Talakadugonda, 'conqueror of Talakad'. With Gangavadi in hand, the Hoysalas ruled the whole southern Karnataka plateau.

Vishnuvardhana had been born a Jain, but under the influence of the philosopher Ramanuja he came to support Vaishnavism, while his queen Shantala Devi and others in his family stayed Jain. To celebrate his success against the Cholas he built the Chennakesava temple at Belur, dedicated to Vishnu and dated to 1117 in the Hoysala Empire article. Its richly carved stone set the style now called Hoysala architecture, and the Hoysaleswara temple at the royal capital, Halebidu, followed around 1121. These temples showed that the Hoysalas were no longer minor chiefs but kings with imperial ambitions.

Vishnuvardhana also tried to break free of his overlord, the Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI. His armies met Chalukya forces at Kannegala around 1118, but around 1122 he was defeated by the Sinda chief Achugi, a Chalukya commander, and had to accept Chalukya overlordship for a time. After Vikramaditya VI died, Chalukya power weakened. By about 1140 Vishnuvardhana had recaptured Hangal, Uchchangi and Bankapura, strongholds in what is now northern Karnataka. The Hoysala kingdom was pushing north toward the Tungabhadra, into the old Chalukya heartland.

As the Chalukya empire collapsed in the 1180s, the Hoysalas and the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri raced to take its lands. Around 1187-1189 the Yadava king Bhillama V seized the old Chalukya capital, Kalyani. Veera Ballala II, Hoysala king from 1173, marched north and defeated Bhillama's army at Soratur and Lakkundi, in present-day Gadag district, around 1191 (the Seuna dynasty article places the battle in the late 1180s). The Yadavas were pushed back beyond the Malaprabha and Krishna rivers, which became the Hoysala-Yadava border for about two decades.

With the Chalukyas gone and the Yadavas beaten back, Veera Ballala II no longer needed to acknowledge any overlord. Around 1192 he crowned himself emperor over the Karnataka region; the Hoysala Empire article dates the declaration of independence to 1193. He ruled from Halebidu (Dwarasamudra), where the Kedareshwara temple was built in his reign, and he patronised Kannada poets such as Janna and Rudrabhatta. For a while, in one historian's phrase, the Hoysalas were paramount throughout most of the Kannada-speaking Deccan, from the Kaveri valley north to the Krishna.

The northern border did not hold. The Yadava king Simhana II, the greatest ruler of his dynasty, attacked while the Hoysalas were busy with wars in the Tamil south. Yadava inscriptions appear south of the Malaprabha from 1202, and by 1213 they had annexed most of present-day Dharwad district. Banavasi fell before 1215, and by 1220 the whole area north of the Tungabhadra was in Yadava hands; the article on Ballala II dates the main loss to after about 1212. The Hoysala kingdom shrank back toward the southern plateau, and its kings turned their ambitions south instead.

Around 1216 the Pandya king Maravarman Sundara Pandya invaded the Chola kingdom and drove King Kulothunga III into exile. The Chola king asked the Hoysalas for help. Ballala II sent an army under his son, the future Narasimha II, which repulsed the Pandyas and put Kulothunga back on his throne. Ballala took titles such as Cholarajyapratishtacharya, 'establisher of the Chola kingdom', and Dakshina Chakravarti, 'emperor of the south', and gained direct control of parts of the Kaveri plains around Srirangam. From now on the Hoysalas were arbiters of Tamil politics.

Under Narasimha II and his son Vira Someshwara the Hoysalas played the Cholas and Pandyas against each other. The Hoysala Empire article says Kannanur Kuppam, near Srirangam, became a provincial capital around 1225; the article on Someshwara says he founded his capital there after 1235 and named it Vikramapura. He conquered Magadai Mandalam in 1236 and switched sides between the Tamil kings as it suited him, and they called him 'Mamadi', uncle. With a royal seat on the Kaveri, the Hoysala realm stretched from the Western Ghats deep into Tamil country.

In 1254 Vira Someshwara split his kingdom between two sons. Narasimha III ruled the Karnataka heartland from Halebidu, while Ramanatha ruled the Tamil possessions from Kannanur. Someshwara himself stayed at Kannanur with Ramanatha and was later killed in a war with the Pandya king Sadayavarman Sundara Pandyan I, who was building a new Pandya empire. The division weakened the dynasty at a dangerous moment. Hoysala dominance in the south, strongest between about 1220 and 1245, faded as the Pandyas rose, and the kingdom was increasingly confined to the Karnataka plateau.

Veera Ballala III, king from 1292, recovered some lost Tamil territory and fought off the Yadavas, defeating them at Holalkere around 1305. But a new power had reached the Deccan: the Delhi Sultanate. After subduing Devagiri and Warangal, Sultan Alauddin Khalji sent his general Malik Kafur south. His army besieged the Hoysala capital, Halebidu, from 25 February 1311. Ballala accepted defeat, handed over great wealth, agreed to pay annual tribute and sent his son to Delhi. Kafur then pushed on to plunder the Pandya kingdom. The Hoysalas survived, but as tributaries of Delhi.

In the 1320s the Tughluq sultans of Delhi annexed the Deccan kingdoms one by one: Warangal fell in 1323 and the small Kampili kingdom on the Tungabhadra around 1327-1328. Around 1327 a Tughluq army sacked Halebidu for a second time. Ballala III retreated to Tiruvannamalai, in the Tamil country, and kept up the resistance from there. By about 1336 every other Hindu kingdom of the south had fallen, and the Hoysala king was the last of the old dynasties still standing. Two officers who had served him, Harihara and Bukka, now administered his northern lands.

In 1335 the Delhi governor of Madurai, Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, declared an independent Madurai Sultanate in the far south. The aged Ballala III made war on it. Around 1342-1343 he fought Sultan Ghiyas-ud-Din Damghani at Kannanur Koppam, near Srirangam, and came close to victory, but he was captured and killed; the Madurai Sultanate article says his body was displayed on the walls of Madurai. Some sources date his death to 8 September 1342, others to 1343. With the king gone, Hoysala resistance collapsed.

Ballala III's son, Veera Ballala IV, held the title for a few years, but he is said to have met a similar end around 1346. In the north, Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family, who had served the Hoysala king as commanders, had been administering Hoysala territory since about 1336 and had founded a new state at Vijayanagara. By 1346 the Hoysala kingdom was gone, merged into the Vijayanagara realm. That year Queen Krishnayitayi and Harihara I made grants to the Sringeri monastery on the same day, a sign of the handover. The Hoysala heartland became the core of the new empire.
